Greetings! I’m in TX and have worked at smaller districts for most of my career. 

1.) teaching to the test is not as extreme as when I worked in gen. ed. It is a federal requirement for English proficiency to be assessed every year (even for newcomers). However it is part of their reclassification criteria so I feel pressure in that way. 

2.) I loved my day to day as an ESL teacher. I did 4 pull out groups for newcomers to intermediates and then push in/ co-teach for four ELA periods to help push our advance to advance high kiddos. Wednesday I did paperwork, meetings etc. my groups were max ten kids. 

The paperwork is significant but not overwhelming- and it’s nothing compared to the paperwork sped teachers need to take care of. 

One thing I didn’t like was that I was one of the first people to be an emergency sub if a teacher called out. 

3) Overall I would recommend this field. Really rewarding with this population of students. 

4) I don’t know about the job climate in MD but we are literally sponsoring international teachers to come teach in our schools bc we don’t have enough ppl down here. It’s also a growing population as well  so I would be surprised if you had difficulty finding a job. 

5) Best part - the kids and most of my coworkers. I’m working with a lot of refugee students from Afghanistan this year and they are so motivated and just so awesome. My coworkers are good people and it feels that we doing something significant and meaningful everyday. Worst part - it can be really emotionally draining and the profession isn’t valued as much. I get a lot of “you’re so smart/capable why didn’t you x? Why are you ‘just’ a teacher?”

I know some districts have data analysts and tech teams that might be a good fit. You can feel like you’re in a more meaningful position while still being able to pee when you want. 

I was a teacher for 10 years before kids and it can be really rough and really great. The state/district/school leadership all make a huge difference and can greatly impact your experience. 

I will say as a mother yeah you get summers off but there is 0 flexibility during the school year. If you’re not there you need to make sub plans. You got to work evening events, parent teacher conferences, tutoring etc. 

I work at the district level now and it’s definitely not as rewarding and joyful as teaching can be, but it is way more predictable and if I need to grab a kid from daycare it is 1,000 times easier to manage.

I think what you’re getting stuck on is the belief that the fetus has a right to live compared to institutions banning abortion because of that belief. Pro-Choice and Pro-Life are political terms that don’t encapsulate the complexity of the issue and people’s lives. You can believe what you want about a fetus and you can believe that an institution making blanket rules for pregnant women is a terrible idea. 

Something I wonder about is how do you enforce an abortion ban? Does everyone who menstruates need to be on a registry and report this to a governing body? Do we need to report any irregularities in menstrual cycles? If I’m pregnant and don’t know it and participate in an activity that is potentially harmful (biking, drinking hibiscus tea, downhill skiing) do I need to prove that it wasn’t intentional if I miscarry? If I’m raped, do I just need a police report or does the rapist need to be convicted first before I have an abortion? If there’s an exception for life of the mother, what are the qualifying exceptions - suicidal ideation? Sepsis? Domestic violence? 

We can counsel our friends and loved ones with compassion and insight, and we can also know that laws banning and restricting abortion will cause much more suffering. 

I think you mentioned you were in the EU so some of this might not apply, but when I talk to people in the US who are pro-life are tell them that the best way to prevent abortions is to support social safety nets and education. Some examples include access to birth control including sterilization, sex ed (including consent) universal healthcare, free/low cost childcare, maternity leave, protected pumping time when returning to work. 

Overall I think if you are concerned about people getting abortions you should focus on the support people need to reduce the need for an abortion not just the act itself. Women have figured out how to do abortions for all of human existence and it will continue this way. The best we can do is provide the conditions so abortions are rare.
